title: Rootly Drops Small PR Rule as Agentic AI Changes Code Review Economics
gist: Incident-management vendor Rootly has abandoned the small-pull-request discipline it enforced for two years, arguing that AI agents write in whole features rather than increments, so diff size no longer predicts risk and 'blast radius' does. The article generalises the shift: Rootly built an internal AI reviewer that scores risk rather than mimicking a human reviewer, moved the real safety gate from merge to progressive feature-flag rollout, and reserves human-written PR sections for the context an agent cannot supply — with Rewind, QCon London 2026 and Patrick Debois cited as evidence the industry is converging on the same conclusion.

insights.claim: Rootly enforced a strict small-pull-request culture with stacked PRs and atomic changes capped at a few hundred lines for two years, then dropped the rule outright once AI agents began generating most of its code.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: A named engineering org publicly retiring a canonical best practice is an early marker that AI-era tooling vendors selling 'faster PR review' are optimising a shrinking problem.
insights.locator: In the post, Rootly co-founder and CTO

insights.claim: AI coding agents think in features rather than increments, emitting migrations, models, services, controllers, tests and frontend components as one complete implementation, which structurally defeats any line-count-based review policy.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Any dev-tool whose value proposition assumes small, human-sized diffs — review queues, diff viewers, per-line metrics — faces a shrinking unit of work to price against.
insights.locator: He writes that AI agents have changed the equation

insights.claim: The small-PR rule was an optimisation for human writing speed, so once AI removed that constraint the rule converted from a benefit into pure process overhead.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: A reusable test for which engineering practices survive agentic coding: ask which human bottleneck the practice was compensating for, then check whether AI removed it.
insights.locator: They figured out that the small-PR rule was optimised

insights.claim: Forcing AI agents to emit stacked PRs produced technically correct but contextually worse reviews, because comments on one PR depended on decisions made in another and reviewers had to reconstruct context across multiple tabs.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Retrofitting agent output into human-shaped workflow artefacts is an actively negative-value engineering effort — a failure mode to watch in dev-tool roadmaps.
insights.locator: The post describes how attempts to make AI agents

insights.claim: Rootly now assesses blast radius instead of PR size, with feature flags and rollback capability taking precedence over line counts as the governing safety metric.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Demand shifts from review-speed tooling toward feature-flag, progressive-delivery and rollback infrastructure — the layer that actually contains agent-authored risk.
insights.quote: The size of the diff stopped being the useful signal. The blast radius is.

insights.claim: AI-generated defects are context bugs rather than logic bugs: the code executes correctly but is applied to the wrong thing, such as a migration dropping a column still used by a background job or a service writing to a table another team reads from.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Static analysis and unit tests will not catch the dominant class of agent failure; the addressable market is cross-system context and dependency mapping, not syntax checking.
insights.quote: AI bugs are context bugs. The code works, but it is applied to the wrong thing.

insights.claim: Rewind, a backup and versioning provider, adopted Rootly's risk-based model in its AI code review tool Diff Vader, which assigns a risk label to every PR based on review findings rather than on lines changed.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Second adopter of the same model within months signals a nascent category standard — risk-labelled PRs — that incumbent SCM vendors have not yet productised.
insights.quote: a PR's risk has almost nothing to do with its line count
insights.locator: Rewind, a backup and versioning provider

themes.theme: Purpose-built AI reviewer, not a human mimic

insights.claim: Rootly built an internal AI code reviewer that scores every PR on risk assessment, standardisation and confidence, and returns specific findings grouped by severity rather than a raw diff.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Structured, scored review output is becoming the interface between agents and humans — a build-vs-buy gap that vendors like Diff Vader are moving to fill.
insights.locator: The company built an internal AI code reviewer

insights.claim: The design principle behind Rootly's reviewer is that it deliberately does not try to be a human reviewer; it answers a single question per PR about what user-facing behaviour would break if the change carried a bug.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Contrarian to most AI-review products, which market human-equivalent review; the narrower single-question framing is cheaper to run and easier to evaluate.
insights.quote: if this change has a bug, what user-facing behaviour breaks?
insights.locator: instead, it answers one question per PR

insights.claim: Rootly's reviewer separates changes that alter what the system does from changes that only affect how fast or how something looks, assigning a different risk profile to each class.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: A cheap triage heuristic teams can implement without buying anything — behaviour-changing versus cosmetic — that sets the bar competing tools must clear.
insights.locator: The AI reviewer flags changes that alter

themes.theme: Safety boundary moves from merge to rollout

insights.claim: At Rootly every significant feature now ships behind a feature flag and is merged to production switched off, moving the safety boundary from merge time to rollout time.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Feature-flag and progressive-delivery platforms become load-bearing infrastructure rather than an optional nicety as agent-authored code volume rises.
insights.locator: Rousseau emphasises how the use of feature flags

insights.claim: Rootly's real code review happens during a staged rollout sequence — the team first, then a handful of customers, then 10 percent, then everyone — rather than in the pull request.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Concrete rollout ladder to benchmark other AI-heavy engineering orgs against; observability and incident tooling capture the value that review tooling loses.
insights.locator: The real review happens during progressive rollout

insights.claim: Rootly's CTO has argued separately that teams should stop trying to review AI's code faster and bet on rollbacks instead, framing production-side safety as the primary control rather than pre-merge inspection.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Directly against the prevailing AI-code-review pitch; if this view spreads, spend rotates from review copilots to rollback, flagging and incident response.
insights.quote: Stop Trying to Review AI's Code Faster: Bet on Rollbacks Instead
insights.locator: He wrote more about this shift toward production-side safety

insights.claim: Rootly explicitly instructs AI assistants not to generate the 'Why and What' sections of a PR description, reserving them for the human who prompted the agent so the business motivation and scope are captured from outside the model.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Defines where human labour retains value in an agentic pipeline — intent and business rationale, not code inspection — which is where accountability and audit tooling will attach.
insights.locator: Rootly explicitly instructs AI assistants not to generate

insights.claim: Rootly requires every pull request to describe how to safely undo itself, including any data fixes, making reversibility a mandatory authoring artefact rather than an after-the-fact scramble.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable control for teams shipping agent code; also a template for what compliance regimes may eventually demand of AI-authored changes.
insights.quote: Every PR needs to describe how to safely undo itself, including any data fixes.
insights.locator: Every PR needs to describe how to safely undo itself

themes.theme: Industry converging: PRs as anti-pattern at agent speed

insights.claim: At QCon London 2026 Michael Webster argued that headless AI agents producing massive pull requests create a severe bottleneck for human reviewers and introduce persistent technical debt.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Human review throughput, not model capability, is emerging as the binding constraint on AI-driven software delivery — the bottleneck any tooling investment must target.
insights.locator: In a presentation at QCon London 2026

insights.claim: Patrick Debois, widely credited as the godfather of DevOps and now DevRel at Tessl, argued at AI Native DevCon London in June 2026 that PR-based workflows are an anti-pattern inside enterprises once teams move at agent speed, because PRs exist to earn trust between contributors who are not strategically aligned.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: If internal teams abandon PR gates, the git-forge review surface that GitHub and GitLab monetise loses centrality inside enterprises even as open source keeps it.
insights.locator: Debois argued that pull requests make sense in open source

insights.claim: Measurable per-token agent costs are imposing process discipline that was previously impossible, because inefficiency that was invisible in human workflows now appears directly on the bill.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Token spend becomes the first hard, line-item metric of engineering waste — a new budget line finance can police and a wedge for FinOps-style tooling aimed at AI coding.
insights.quote: With humans alone, it was hard to see inefficiencies, but now, with measurable token costs, waste literally shows up in the bill.
